claim: Seasonal influenza infects between 10% and 20% of the human population every year.
source: Seasonal influenza infects between 10% and 20% of the human population every year, causing an estimated 250,000 to 500,000 deaths annually (Influenza Fact sheet, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Influenza Fact sheet, 2009

claim: Seasonal influenza causes an estimated 250,000 to 500,000 deaths annually.
source: Seasonal influenza infects between 10% and 20% of the human population every year, causing an estimated 250,000 to 500,000 deaths annually (Influenza Fact sheet, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Influenza Fact sheet, 2009

claim: Individuals develop long-lasting immunity to particular influenza strains after infection.
source: Although individuals develop long-lasting immunity to particular influenza strains after infection, antigenic mutations to the influenza virus genome result in proteins that are recognized to a lesser degree by the human immune system, leaving individuals susceptible to future infection.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about immune response to influenza

claim: Antigenic mutations to the influenza virus genome result in proteins that are recognized to a lesser degree by the human immune system.
source: Although individuals develop long-lasting immunity to particular influenza strains after infection, antigenic mutations to the influenza virus genome result in proteins that are recognized to a lesser degree by the human immune system, leaving individuals susceptible to future infection.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about antigenic drift

claim: The influenza virus population continually evolves in antigenic phenotype in a process known as antigenic drift.
source: The influenza virus population continually evolves in antigenic phenotype in a process known as antigenic drift.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about influenza evolution

claim: A large proportion of the disease burden of influenza stems from antigenic drift.
source: A large proportion of the disease burden of influenza stems from antigenic drift, which allows individuals to be infected multiple times throughout their lives.
evidence: Logical inference from the fact that antigenic drift allows repeated infections

claim: Antigenic drift causes efficacy of a fixed vaccine formulation against circulating viruses to decline over time.
source: Although influenza vaccines may lack efficacy for a variety of reasons (Osterholm et al., 2012), antigenic drift causes efficacy of a fixed vaccine formulation against circulating viruses to decline over time.
evidence: Supported by citation to Osterholm et al., 2012 and established knowledge

claim: Before 2009, there were four major lineages of influenza circulating within the human population: the H3N2 and H1N1 subtypes of influenza A, and the Victoria and Yamagata lineages of influenza B.
source: Before 2009, there were four major lineages of influenza circulating within the human population: the H3N2 and H1N1 subtypes of influenza A, and the Victoria and Yamagata lineages of influenza B.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about influenza lineages

claim: Victoria and Yamagata lineages of influenza B diverged from a single lineage prior to 1980.
source: In the case of influenza B, Victoria (B/Vic) and Yamagata (B/Yam) refer to antigenically distinct lineages which diverged from a single lineage prior to 1980 (Rota et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rota et al., 1990

claim: Mutations to the HA1 region of the hemagglutinin protein are thought to drive the majority of antigenic drift in the influenza virus.
source: Mutations to the HA1 region of the hemagglutinin protein are thought to drive the majority of antigenic drift in the influenza virus (Wiley et al., 1981; Nelson and Holmes, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wiley et al., 1981 and Nelson and Holmes, 2007

claim: Experimental characterization of antigenic phenotype is possible through the hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay.
source: Experimental characterization of antigenic phenotype is possible through the hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay (Hirst, 1943), which measures the cross-reactivity of one virus strain to serum raised against another strain through challenge or vaccination.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirst, 1943

claim: The HI assay measures the cross-reactivity of one virus strain to serum raised against another strain through challenge or vaccination.
source: Experimental characterization of antigenic phenotype is possible through the hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay (Hirst, 1943), which measures the cross-reactivity of one virus strain to serum raised against another strain through challenge or vaccination.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirst, 1943 and established knowledge

claim: Sera raised against older strains react poorly to more recent viruses.
source: Sera raised against older strains react poorly to more recent viruses resulting in new strains having a selective advantage over previously established strains.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about antigenic evolution

claim: The results of many HI assays across a multitude of viruses of a single subtype can be combined to yield a two-dimensional map, quantifying antigenic similarity and distance.
source: The results of many HI assays across a multitude of viruses of a single subtype can be combined to yield a two-dimensional map, quantifying antigenic similarity and distance (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2004

claim: The antigenic map of influenza A/H3N2 has shown substantial evolution of the influenza virus population since its emergence in 1968.
source: The antigenic map of influenza A/H3N2 has shown substantial evolution of the influenza virus population since its emergence in 1968.
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2004 in the preceding sentence

claim: Evolution of antigenic phenotype in A/H3N2 appears punctuated with episodes of more rapid innovation interspersed by periods of relative stasis.
source: Evolution of antigenic phenotype appears punctuated with episodes of more rapid innovation interspersed by periods of relative stasis, whereas genetic evolution appears more continuous (Smith et al., 2004), suggesting that a relatively small number of genetic changes or combinations of genetic changes may drive changes in antigenic phenotype (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2004

claim: Genetic evolution of A/H3N2 appears more continuous than antigenic evolution.
source: Evolution of antigenic phenotype appears punctuated with episodes of more rapid innovation interspersed by periods of relative stasis, whereas genetic evolution appears more continuous (Smith et al., 2004), suggesting that a relatively small number of genetic changes or combinations of genetic changes may drive changes in antigenic phenotype (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2004

claim: A relatively small number of genetic changes or combinations of genetic changes may drive changes in antigenic phenotype.
source: Evolution of antigenic phenotype appears punctuated with episodes of more rapid innovation interspersed by periods of relative stasis, whereas genetic evolution appears more continuous (Smith et al., 2004), suggesting that a relatively small number of genetic changes or combinations of genetic changes may drive changes in antigenic phenotype (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2004 and Koel et al., 2013

claim: The process of antigenic drift results in the rapid turnover of the virus population.
source: The process of antigenic drift results in the rapid turnover of the virus population, so that despite mutation, genetic diversity among contemporaneous viruses remains low.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about influenza population dynamics

claim: Despite mutation, genetic diversity among contemporaneous influenza viruses remains low.
source: The process of antigenic drift results in the rapid turnover of the virus population, so that despite mutation, genetic diversity among contemporaneous viruses remains low.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about influenza population dynamics

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of influenza shows a characteristically 'spindly' tree with a single predominant trunk lineage and transitory side branches that persist for only 1–5 years.
source: Such population turnover is supported by phylogenetic analysis that shows a characteristically 'spindly' tree with a single predominant trunk lineage and transitory side branches that persist for only 1–5 years (Fitch et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fitch et al., 1997

claim: A two-dimensional model has better predictive power than models of lower or higher dimension in all four influenza lineages.
source: We find that a two-dimensional model has better predictive power than models of lower or higher dimension in all four influenza lineages (models 1–5; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1 showing test errors across different dimensional models

claim: The 2D BMDS model yields an average absolute predictive error of between 0.78 and 0.91 log2 HI titers across influenza lineages.
source: We find that this 2D model performs well, yielding an average absolute predictive error of between 0.78 and 0.91 log2 HI titers across influenza lineages (model 2; Table 1), in line with the results of Smith et al. (2004).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1, model 2

claim: There is a correlation between amino acid mutations and antigenic distance in influenza viruses.
source: Here, we examine pairwise relationships between viruses and observe a correlation between amino acid mutations and antigenic distance (Figure 1) and a similar correlation between phylogenetic distance, measured in years, and antigenic distance (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: There is a correlation between phylogenetic distance, measured in years, and antigenic distance in influenza viruses.
source: Here, we examine pairwise relationships between viruses and observe a correlation between amino acid mutations and antigenic distance (Figure 1) and a similar correlation between phylogenetic distance, measured in years, and antigenic distance (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: The magnitudes of the coefficients of determination R2 between genetic relationships and antigenic distances are low.
source: However, the magnitudes of the coefficients of determination R2are low (Figure 1), suggesting that genetic relationships alone will not completely resolve antigenic distances.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: Genetic relationships alone will not completely resolve antigenic distances.
source: However, the magnitudes of the coefficients of determination R2are low (Figure 1), suggesting that genetic relationships alone will not completely resolve antigenic distances.
evidence: Inferred from the low R2 values shown in Figure 1

claim: Including both systematic drift and phylogenetic diffusion results in a small increase in predictive accuracy of between 0.02 and 0.08 log2 HI titers compared to drift alone.
source: We examine the effects of including only systematic drift (model 6; Table 1) and systematic drift plus phylogenetic diffusion (model 7; Table 1), finding a small increase in predictive accuracy of between 0.02 and 0.08 log2 HI titers when both processes are included.
evidence: Supported by comparison of models 6 and 7 in Table 1

claim: Estimating serum potencies improves test error by between 0.01 and 0.12 log2 HI titers.
source: We find that estimating serum potencies improves test error further (model 8, Table 1), with improvements of between 0.01 and 0.12 log2 HI titers.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1, model 8

claim: Including virus avidities with fixed serum potencies results in improvements of between 0.02 and 0.09 log2 HI titers.
source: We find that including virus avidities further improves test error, either with fixed serum potencies (model 9, Table 1) or with estimated serum potencies (model 10, Table 1). With fixed serum potencies, the inclusion of virus avidities results in improvements of between 0.02 and 0.09 log2 HI titers and with estimated serum potencies, the inclusion of virus avidities results in improvements of between 0.01 and 0.05 log2 HI titers.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1, model 9

claim: Including virus avidities with estimated serum potencies results in improvements of between 0.01 and 0.05 log2 HI titers.
source: We find that including virus avidities further improves test error, either with fixed serum potencies (model 9, Table 1) or with estimated serum potencies (model 10, Table 1). With fixed serum potencies, the inclusion of virus avidities results in improvements of between 0.02 and 0.09 log2 HI titers and with estimated serum potencies, the inclusion of virus avidities results in improvements of between 0.01 and 0.05 log2 HI titers.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1, model 10

claim: The average absolute error in predicted log2 HI titer is nearly constant with antigenic distance.
source: We find that the average absolute error in predicted log2 HI titer is nearly constant with antigenic distance (Pearson correlation, r = 0.098), thus supporting our model assumption that the drop in log2 titer is proportional to the Euclidean distance separating viruses and sera on the antigenic map.
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis

claim: The absolute error in predicted titer is nearly constant with time.
source: Additionally, we find that the absolute error in predicted titer is nearly constant with time (Pearson correlation, r = −0.007).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis

claim: Virus distances have, on average, a 50% credible interval of ±0.45 antigenic units for A/H3N2.
source: We estimate that virus distances have, on average, a 50% credible interval of ±0.45 antigenic units for A/H3N2, ±0.57 units for A/H1N1, ±0.76 units for B/Vic, and ±0.65 units for B/Yam.
evidence: Supported by Bayesian credible interval estimates from the model

claim: Virus distances have, on average, a 50% credible interval of ±0.57 antigenic units for A/H1N1.
source: We estimate that virus distances have, on average, a 50% credible interval of ±0.45 antigenic units for A/H3N2, ±0.57 units for A/H1N1, ±0.76 units for B/Vic, and ±0.65 units for B/Yam.
evidence: Supported by Bayesian credible interval estimates from the model

claim: Virus distances have, on average, a 50% credible interval of ±0.76 antigenic units for B/Vic.
source: We estimate that virus distances have, on average, a 50% credible interval of ±0.45 antigenic units for A/H3N2, ±0.57 units for A/H1N1, ±0.76 units for B/Vic, and ±0.65 units for B/Yam.
evidence: Supported by Bayesian credible interval estimates from the model

claim: Virus distances have, on average, a 50% credible interval of ±0.65 antigenic units for B/Yam.
source: We estimate that virus distances have, on average, a 50% credible interval of ±0.45 antigenic units for A/H3N2, ±0.57 units for A/H1N1, ±0.76 units for B/Vic, and ±0.65 units for B/Yam.
evidence: Supported by Bayesian credible interval estimates from the model

claim: Over the time period of 1968 to 2011, influenza A/H3N2 shows substantially more antigenic evolution than is exhibited by A/H1N1 over the course of 1977 to 2009 or B/Vic and B/Yam over the course of 1986 to 2011.
source: Over the time period of 1968 to 2011, influenza A/H3N2 shows substantially more antigenic evolution than is exhibited by A/H1N1 over the course of 1977 to 2009 or B/Vic and B/Yam over the course of 1986 to 2011.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3

claim: Prominent antigenic clusters are observed in A/H3N2 and A/H1N1.
source: We observe prominent antigenic clusters in A/H3N2 and A/H1N1, but less prominent, though still apparent, clustering in B/Vic and B/Yam.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: Less prominent, though still apparent, clustering is observed in B/Vic and B/Yam.
source: We observe prominent antigenic clusters in A/H3N2 and A/H1N1, but less prominent, though still apparent, clustering in B/Vic and B/Yam.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: Antigenic clusters show high genetic similarity.
source: Antigenic clusters show high genetic similarity, so that we observe very few mutation events leading to each cluster, rather than the repeated emergence of clusters.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: Two clusters in A/H3N2 (Victoria/75 and Beijing/89) appear to be evolutionary dead-ends.
source: This analysis makes the fate of antigenic clusters obvious, with two clusters in A/H3N2 (Victoria/75 and Beijing/89) appearing to be evolutionary dead-ends.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: Influenza A/H3N2 evolved along antigenic dimension 1 at an estimated rate of 1.01 antigenic units per year.
source: We find that influenza A/H3N2 evolved along antigenic dimension 1 at an estimated rate of 1.01 antigenic units per year (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2

claim: Occasional large jumps in antigenic phenotype are observed in A/H3N2, corresponding to cluster transitions.
source: However, we observe occasional large jumps in antigenic phenotype (Figure 3), corresponding to cluster transitions identified by Smith et al. (2004).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and citation to Smith et al., 2004

claim: Influenza A/H1N1 evolved at a rate of 0.62 antigenic units per year.
source: Influenza A/H1N1 evolved at a rate of 0.62 units per year, but showed a similar pattern of punctuated antigenic evolution with occasional larger jumps in phenotype, such as the emergence of the Solomon Islands/06 cluster.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2

claim: Influenza B/Victoria evolved at a rate of 0.42 antigenic units per year.
source: Influenza B/Victoria and B/Yamagata evolved slower still, with mean estimated rates 0.42 units per year and 0.32 units per year, respectively.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2

claim: Influenza B/Yamagata evolved at a rate of 0.32 antigenic units per year.
source: Influenza B/Victoria and B/Yamagata evolved slower still, with mean estimated rates 0.42 units per year and 0.32 units per year, respectively.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2

claim: Punctuated evolution is less obvious in B/Yam and B/Vic compared to A/H3N2 and A/H1N1.
source: Punctuated evolution is less obvious in B/Yam and B/Vic compared to A/H3N2 and A/H1N1, but antigenic clusters are still apparent, with recent transitions to the Brisbane/08 cluster in B/Vic (Barr et al., 2010) and to the Wisconsin/10 cluster in B/Yam (Klimov et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and citations

claim: A minor lineage of B/Vic, denoted B/Hubei-Songzi/51/2008, has persisted through 2011, while remaining antigenically distinct from B/Brisbane/60/2008 viruses.
source: Interestingly, a minor lineage of B/Vic, denoted B/Hubei-Songzi/51/2008 (Barr et al., 2010), has persisted through 2011, while remaining antigenically distinct from B/Brisbane/60/2008 viruses (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and citation to Barr et al., 2010

claim: Significantly different drift rates are observed between influenza lineages.
source: Although we observe significantly different drift rates between lineages, we observe less variation in diffusion volatility (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2

claim: Less variation in diffusion volatility is observed between lineages compared to drift rates.
source: Although we observe significantly different drift rates between lineages, we observe less variation in diffusion volatility (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2

claim: All four influenza lineages exhibit similar levels of standing antigenic variation.
source: This is reflected in Figure 3, where all four lineages exhibit similar levels of standing antigenic variation, despite A/H3N2 drifting more quickly in antigenic phenotype.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: Influenza A/H3N2 has a characteristically spindly tree showing rapid turnover of the virus population.
source: Influenza A/H3N2 has a characteristically spindly tree showing rapid turnover of the virus population, while A/H1N1 and B have trees that show greater degrees of viral coexistance (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4

claim: A/H1N1 and B have trees that show greater degrees of viral coexistence compared to A/H3N2.
source: Influenza A/H3N2 has a characteristically spindly tree showing rapid turnover of the virus population, while A/H1N1 and B have trees that show greater degrees of viral coexistance (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4

claim: Neτ broadly correlates with the rate of antigenic drift.
source: We see that Neτ broadly correlates with the rate of antigenic drift (Table 2), with A/H3N2 showing fast drift and reduced effective population size as expected from basic epidemiological models (Bedford et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2 and citation to Bedford et al., 2012

claim: A/H3N2 shows fast drift and reduced effective population size as expected from basic epidemiological models.
source: We see that Neτ broadly correlates with the rate of antigenic drift (Table 2), with A/H3N2 showing fast drift and reduced effective population size as expected from basic epidemiological models (Bedford et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2 and citation to Bedford et al., 2012

claim: Antigenic drift results in the replacement of antigenically primitive lineages by antigenically advanced lineages, thereby reducing genealogical diversity.
source: Antigenic drift results in the replacement of antigenically primitive lineages by antigenically advanced lineages, thereby reducing genealogical diversity.
evidence: Logical inference from the observed patterns of antigenic evolution and phylogenetic structure

claim: A faster rate of antigenic drift is observed in influenza A/H3N2 than in A/H1N1 or either lineage of influenza B.
source: Thus, we observe a faster rate of antigenic drift in influenza A/H3N2 than in A/H1N1 or either lineage of influenza B.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2 and Figure 3

claim: Rates of antigenic drift may be influenced by both the fundamental reproductive number R0 and the rate at which mutation decreases cross-immunity.
source: Previous work using general epidemiological models has suggested that rates of antigenic drift may be influenced by both the fundamental reproductive number R0 and the rate at which mutation decreases cross-immunity (Gog and Grenfell, 2002; Lin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gog and Grenfell, 2002 and Lin et al., 2003

claim: Models specific to influenza evolution ascribe differences in the rate of antigenic drift of A/H3N2 relative to A/H1N1 and influenza B to either greater R0 or greater mutation rate.
source: Correspondingly, models specific to influenza evolution ascribe differences in the rate of antigenic drift of A/H3N2 relative to A/H1N1 and influenza B to either greater R0 or greater mutation rate (Ferguson et al., 2003; Bedford et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2003 and Bedford et al., 2012

claim: Greater heterogeneity in year-to-year antigenic drift is observed in type A than in type B lineages.
source: We observe greater heterogeneity in year-to-year antigenic drift in type A than in type B lineages (Figure 5B), with standard deviation of year-to-year antigenic drift equal to 0.97 units in A/H3N2, 0.66 units in A/H1N1, 0.46 units in B/Vic and 0.26 units in B/Yam.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The standard deviation of year-to-year antigenic drift is 0.97 units in A/H3N2.
source: We observe greater heterogeneity in year-to-year antigenic drift in type A than in type B lineages (Figure 5B), with standard deviation of year-to-year antigenic drift equal to 0.97 units in A/H3N2, 0.66 units in A/H1N1, 0.46 units in B/Vic and 0.26 units in B/Yam.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: A significant correlation exists between rate of antigenic drift and relative incidence across the four influenza lineages.
source: We begin by comparing overall rates of antigenic drift (Figure 3, Table 2) to overall levels of seasonal incidence across influenza lineages, finding a significant correlation between rate of antigenic drift and relative incidence across the four lineages (Pearson correlation, r = 0.97, p = 0.041).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis with p = 0.041

claim: Within each virus lineage, years with pronounced antigenic drift tend to show increased incidence.
source: Within each virus lineage, we find that years with pronounced antigenic drift tend to show increased incidence (Figure 6), finding Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.51, 0.29, 0.44 and 0.14 for A/H3N2, A/H1N1, B/Vic and B/Yam respectively.
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 6

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient between year-to-year drift and incidence is 0.51 for A/H3N2.
source: Within each virus lineage, we find that years with pronounced antigenic drift tend to show increased incidence (Figure 6), finding Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.51, 0.29, 0.44 and 0.14 for A/H3N2, A/H1N1, B/Vic and B/Yam respectively.
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient between year-to-year drift and incidence is 0.29 for A/H1N1.
source: Within each virus lineage, we find that years with pronounced antigenic drift tend to show increased incidence (Figure 6), finding Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.51, 0.29, 0.44 and 0.14 for A/H3N2, A/H1N1, B/Vic and B/Yam respectively.
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient between year-to-year drift and incidence is 0.44 for B/Vic.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient between year-to-year drift and incidence is 0.14 for B/Yam.

evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis

claim: The p-value for the correlation between drift and incidence is 0.056 for A/H3N2.
source: We calculated significance using bootstrap permutation tests finding p-values of 0.056, 0.201, 0.097, and 0.341 respectively.
evidence: Supported by bootstrap permutation test

claim: The p-value for the correlation between drift and incidence is 0.201 for A/H1N1.
source: We calculated significance using bootstrap permutation tests finding p-values of 0.056, 0.201, 0.097, and 0.341 respectively.
evidence: Supported by bootstrap permutation test

claim: The p-value for the correlation between drift and incidence is 0.097 for B/Vic.
source: We calculated significance using bootstrap permutation tests finding p-values of 0.056, 0.201, 0.097, and 0.341 respectively.
evidence: Supported by bootstrap permutation test

claim: The p-value for the correlation between drift and incidence is 0.341 for B/Yam.
source: We calculated significance using bootstrap permutation tests finding p-values of 0.056, 0.201, 0.097, and 0.341 respectively.
evidence: Supported by bootstrap permutation test

claim: The p-value for finding the observed degree of correlation across all four lineages is 0.018.
source: We applied a similar bootstrap permutation test to calculate the significance of finding the observed degree of correlation across all four lineages, arriving at a p-value of 0.018.
evidence: Supported by bootstrap permutation test

claim: The observation of periods of pronounced antigenic drift preceding increased incidence in each of the four influenza lineages suggests a causal relationship, in which antigenic evolution drives increased incidence.
source: The fact that we observe periods of pronounced antigenic drift preceding increased incidence in each of the four influenza lineages suggests a causal relationship, in which antigenic evolution drives increased incidence.
evidence: Inferred from the observed correlation between drift and subsequent incidence

claim: Little correlation exists between viral isolate count and estimates of year-to-year drift when combining data across lineages.
source: We controlled for this possibility by testing to see if viral isolate count influences estimates of year-to-year drift by correlating drift between years i and i − 1 against the ratio of the number of isolates from year i to the number of isolates from year i − 1. We found little correlation when combining data across lineages (Figure 7, Pearson's r = −0.01).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 7

claim: The p-value for the correlation between sample count ratio and drift is 0.514 across all lineages.
source: We tested significance following the same bootstrap procedure we used to assess the correlation between drift and incidence, finding a p-value of 0.514.
evidence: Supported by bootstrap permutation test

claim: The p-values for the correlation between sample count ratio and drift are 0.717, 0.246, 0.337, 0.504 for A/H3N2, A/H1N1, B/Vic and B/Yam, respectively.
source: Separating lineages gave p-values of 0.717, 0.246, 0.337, 0.504 for A/H3N2, A/H1N1, B/Vic and B/Yam, respectively.
evidence: Supported by bootstrap permutation test

claim: The results are unbiased with regard to sample count.
source: These findings suggest our results to be unbiased with regard to sample count.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between sample count and drift estimates

claim: The correlation between antigenic drift and viral incidence both across and within influenza lineages suggests a causal role for antigenic drift driving influenza incidence patterns.
source: Furthermore, we observe a correlation between antigenic drift and viral incidence both across and within influenza lineages. The finding that antigenic evolution correlates with subsequent increased incidence within a lineage suggests a causal role for antigenic drift driving influenza incidence patterns.
evidence: Inferred from the observed correlations between drift and incidence

claim: The correlation between incidence and drift suggests the possibility of using HI data at the start of an influenza season to predict which lineage will subsequently predominate.
source: The correlation between incidence and drift further suggests the possibility of using HI data at the start of an influenza season to predict which lineage will subsequently predominate.
evidence: Speculative inference from the observed correlation between drift and incidence

claim: The BMDS model produces results that are strongly congruent with MDS results when using equivalent models.
source: Unsurprisingly, we find that this BMDS model produces results that are strongly congruent with MDS results (Figure 10, Figure 10—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 10

claim: Antigenic cluster locations are consistent between MDS and BMDS methods.
source: Antigenic cluster locations are consistent between methods (Figure 10A–B) and antigenic distances between pairs of viruses are consistent between temporally similar and temporally divergent viruses (Figure 10C–E), suggesting that the resulting maps are consistent at both local and global scales.
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 10

claim: Credible intervals of antigenic distances for the BMDS model remain narrow across the temporal spectrum.
source: Credible intervals of antigenic distances for the BMDS model remain narrow across the temporal spectrum (Figure 10C–E), implying a fair degree of rigidity to the map.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 10

claim: There exist at least two solutions in the assignment of antigenic locations, involving the rotation of clusters HK/68, EN/72 and VI/75.
source: Smith et al. 2004 show that there exist at least two solutions in their assignment of antigenic locations, involving the rotation of clusters HK/68, EN/72 and VI/75 (shown in Figure S2 of [Smith et al., 2004]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2004

claim: The same metastable behavior observed by Smith et al. 2004 is observed in the BMDS analysis.

claim: Including the drift prior on antigenic locations removes the problem of identifiability.
source: We find that including this drift prior on antigenic locations removes the problem of identifiability.

claim: Antigenic locations produced by the drift model remain locally consistent with MDS results between viruses ∼15 years divergent.
source: Antigenic locations produced by this model remain locally consistent with MDS results between viruses ∼15 years divergent, but global comparisons show that this BMDS model has partitioned more variance to the first antigenic dimension (Figure 12, Figure 12—source data 1).

claim: Including the drift prior on antigenic locations often results in greater predictive power.
source: We additionally find that including the drift prior on antigenic locations often results in greater predictive power, with a slight improvement of test error for the A/H1N1, B/Vic, and B/Yam datasets (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of models in Table 1

claim: Estimating virus avidity and serum potency results in a more linear antigenic map.
source: Surprisingly, estimating virus avidity and serum potency results in a more linear antigenic map (Figure 13, Figure 13—source data 1), resembling the appearance of the map incorporating the antigenic drift prior, while preserving local consistency.
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 13

claim: Congruence between MDS and BMDS antigenic locations is generally observed for viruses less than ∼10 years divergent.
source: We generally observe congruence between MDS and BMDS antigenic locations for viruses less than ∼10 years divergent (Figure 13E).
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 13

claim: Viruses 15 or more years divergent always yield threshold titers in the dataset.
source: In this dataset, viruses 15 or more years divergent always yield threshold titers, and hence, their relative locations must be indirectly inferred rather than through direct comparison.
evidence: Observation from the HI data used in the analysis
